hotspots.title: Expanding tray + TPU grippers
hotspots.oneLiner: The phone clamps between the grips, held by soft toothed pads.
hotspots.blurb: Fits anything from about 130 to 170 mm — a plain iPhone through a Galaxy Ultra, case on. The pads hook over the front edge and a shelf along the bottom carries the weight, so it stays put even held above your face.

hotspots.title: nRF52840 module (Ebyte E73-2G4M08S1C)
hotspots.oneLiner: The Bluetooth chip that runs the whole keyboard.
hotspots.blurb: One radio for the whole keyboard means one thing to pair and one battery to charge. It behaves like a single keyboard, not two halves you have to keep in sync.

hotspots.oneLiner: The chip that senses the pointing nub, from under the board.
hotspots.blurb: It reads the nub straight through the circuit board, so nothing rubs and nothing is exposed — no wiper to wear out, no gap for grit to get into.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.dek: A keyboard built around your phone's screen, not bolted on top of it.
paragraphs: Your phone clamps landscape in the middle: the two grips slide on a spring-loaded 2-part tray and pull together to grip it by the short edges, fitting phones from about 130 to 170 mm. Soft TPU grippers with teeth and deep lips hold it mechanically — safe even screen-down — Two grips flank it. You hold the whole thing like a game controller and thumb-type a full 78-key QWERTY. The shell is translucent Atomic-Purple over dark-gray keymats; it looks a bit like a Game Boy Color ate a keyboard.

The keys are metal snap domes — the clicky stainless discs from inside a TV remote. No switches, no stems, nothing to hand-solder: the dome is the switch. And while it has two halves, it isn't a split keyboard. One chip in the right grip runs everything, the left grip is just domes and diodes, and a ribbon cable joins them — so it's one Bluetooth device, one battery, one firmware image.

sections.heading: Why I built this
sections.dek: Physical keyboards are better. Phones are heavy in the wrong place. Mobile gaming already solved that exact problem.
paragraphs: Physical keyboards are just better than typing on a screen. I think a lot of us have felt that way for a long time. And as phones have become more and more central to how we lead our lives, being able to interface with them has only gotten more important — many of us are doing all of our writing, our work, our communication through a phone. When all of that has to go through swipe typing, the phone becomes a bottleneck on your own thoughts. That's not something we have to live with anymore.

I've been strapping physical keyboards to the sides of phones for a long time, and one problem kept coming up over and over again. No matter what I did, it never equalled the quality of what I had in the Sidekick era.

images.alt: A Rii i8 mini wireless keyboard with a trackpad
Mock-up of two mini keyboards flanking a phone in landscape

paragraphs.caption: Where this started: a pair of Rii i8 mini keyboards, one on each side of the phone.

paragraphs: The problem is that phones are just too heavy. The Sidekick's form factor worked because the battery, the compute, and the keyboard were all in the bottom part of the phone, and the screen that slid up was the light part — so the weight rested naturally in the bottom of your hand.

When you strap a keyboard to the bottom or the side of a phone, the weight is always wrong. It's always in the top half. And if you weight the bottom of the keyboard, you don't really fix it — you just end up with something so heavy that it drags your hands down.

Interestingly enough, this problem has already been solved. The exact same problem existed in the mobile gaming community about ten years back, and about six years ago we arrived at the real resolution for it: a Switch-style controller, or what you may think of as a Backbone-style controller. It solves all of these problems.

images.alt: A Backbone-style mobile controller: two grips joined by a telescoping bridge

paragraphs.caption: The mobile-gaming answer: phone in the middle, weight between your hands.

paragraphs: The trick is to place the phone in the middle, in between the two hand grips, so that the weight is centred. This may seem like a trivial improvement. But centring that weight between your hands turns something that is impossible to balance — something that creates immense finger and wrist strain, that you can't really use at all, let alone for long — into a device that can be used comfortably for hours on end.

The mission of Gripster is to take exactly that approach and apply it to the mobile keyboard problem. I've actually been sending sketches and specs for precisely this device over the course of the last decade. I've rarely gotten responses, and I certainly haven't seen any of the mobile keyboard companies produce any of the things I've asked for.

images.alt: Hand-drawn concept sketch: a split QWERTY keyboard on two grips with the phone held in the middle

paragraphs.caption: One of those sketches — keys on the grips, phone in the middle. The centre magnet has since been dropped for a mechanical clamp.

sections.heading: A few things it does differently
sections.dek: Four ideas that make it more than a phone case with buttons glued on.
paragraphs: It fits your phone, not one specific phone. The grips ride a spring-loaded 2-part telescoping tray — like an Abxylute or 8BitDo controller — so you stretch it open, drop the phone in, and let the springs clamp it by the edges. A soft toothed TPU gripper on each grip hooks a lip over the phone's front edge — soft on purpose, so it flexes for your case and can't scratch the glass — so it's held mechanically and is safe even used screen-down over your face; there are no magnets at all. The back is one flat plane, coplanar with the centre tray, with every outside edge softened by a 1.2 mm round.

It looks like a split, but it's one keyboard. A single nRF52840 module in the right grip scans the whole 9×10 matrix; the left grip is passive — domes, diodes, a connector — wired across on one ribbon. That's one thing to pair, one battery to charge, and no two halves trying to find each other.

Nothing gets hand-soldered. The 78 keys are snap domes pressed onto gold pads, and every part that is soldered sits on one side of each board in a single reflow pass. A fab house builds both boards end to end — no iron, no rework.

It's generated, not drawn. One Python file lays out both grips, and the circuit boards, printed shells, firmware keymap, and these renders all fall out of it. A key opening lines up with its pad because the same number placed both — not because I eyeballed it.

Why it isn't a split keyboard

sections.heading: How it works
sections.dek: One matrix, one radio, one battery — all run from the right grip.
paragraphs: It's a single 9×10 matrix — 78 keys — scanned by the E73 (nRF52840) module in the right grip. The left grip has no brain of its own, just domes and one diode per key so chords don't ghost. Half the columns are local to the right grip; the rest, and every row, cross over on a 16-way ribbon. A small simulator walks about 68,500 multi-key combinations and turns up zero ghosts or misses.

Power is one 403040 LiPo (~450–500 mAh) tucked into the left grip, its leads crossing to a charger and slide switch on the right. The switch only cuts the load, so the cell keeps charging over USB-C even with the deck off. The module spends 19 pins on the matrix and one on battery sensing, with a spare I²C bus parked on test pads in case a trackpad ever happens.

It pairs as a single Bluetooth keyboard — no second half to drop. The antenna sits at the top edge, as far from the phone and battery as the board allows, with a clear-out in the copper and a notch in the shell to match.

sections.heading: It all comes out of one Python file
sections.dek: Move a key in one place and its pad, its hole in the shell, and its slot in the firmware all move with it.
paragraphs: Both grips — every key position, dimension, and keep-out — live in one file, deck.py. Everything downstream is generated from it: the KiCad boards, the printed shells, the ZMK keymap. Nothing gets drawn or measured twice.

The 3D parts come from a second script, deck3d.py, built on CadQuery. It reads the layout and the real board placement, so shell openings land on actual pads and cutouts land on actual connectors. Every run checks the whole assembly for watertight parts and collisions before anything ships.
That whole loop is currently green: both boards route clean in KiCad 9, and all nine printed parts pass the watertight and no-collision checks for a stock Ender 3 V2 bed.

sections.heading: Full disclosure: this is a heavily AI-developed project
sections.dek: In goes a prompt, out comes an output — and a test that doesn't rely on AI decides whether it's any good.
paragraphs: I have never before designed a piece of hardware at this level. I don't have an education in PCB design or in electrical engineering. I have previously been a project manager for hardware/software integration projects to the tune of billions of dollars, at major corporations like Microsoft and Axon. But without the aid of AI coding models, this would not have been possible.

My aim here was to see if AI coding models could be applied to solve problems in the real world, in a manner emulating what we've developed for software: in goes a prompt, out comes some output, a test that does not rely on AI determines whether or not that output is good, and the feedback from that test goes back into the AI. Only when the tests are passing is the output deemed good enough to even be viewed by a person.

That's why so much of this repo is checks rather than drawings. The matrix is proven ghost-free by walking about 68,500 multi-key combinations; the boards are held to a clean KiCad DRC; every printed part is tested for watertightness, for collisions against the whole assembly, and for fitting a stock Ender 3 V2 bed. None of those judgements are made by a model — they're made by a script the model has to satisfy.

All of the systems and flows that I used to create this are open source and freely available on GitHub. My hope is that, in addition to scratching my own itch of wanting this very special thing to come into the world to solve my very particular problem, this project can also help kickstart a wave of open-source hardware that we can all iterate on together. Contributions are welcome — I would love to see this project take on a life of its own. Please get in touch if you have any questions.

sections.heading: Build one
sections.dek: It's open hardware — the boards, the shells, the firmware, and the model that generates them all.
paragraphs: Everything's on GitHub under Apache-2.0: the two KiCad boards with a JLCPCB-ready fab package, the printable shells sized for a stock Ender 3 V2, the ZMK firmware, and the deck.py model that spits all of it out. Order the boards turnkey, print the shells, press in the snap domes, and flash the firmware over USB-C.
Want a different layout, grip shape, or keymap? Edit the model and regenerate — the boards, shells, and firmware all follow. Pull requests and build reports welcome.
